Kusuda T.lab_name: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo (Tokyo, Japan)
Kusuda T.role: First author of a 2026 study on CASTOR1, an arginine sensor that restrains mTORC1 in B cells, and lupus-like disease in mice.
Kusuda T.sub: Department of Allergy and Rheumatology, University of Tokyo (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Takeshi Kusuda was first author of a 2026 Atlas study from the University of Tokyo (KUS2026). It gave the arginine sensor CASTOR1 a clear job upstream of mTORC1. Mice without it had more active mTORC1 in B cells, more antibody-making plasma cells, and lupus-like kidney damage. In people with lupus, lower CASTOR1 in plasmablasts went with higher disease activity.

highlights.KUS2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Allergy and Rheumatology at the University of Tokyo.

Laberge RM.lab_name: Buck Institute for Research on Aging (Novato, California, USA)
Laberge RM.role: First author of a 2015 study showing that mTOR drives the inflammatory secretions of senescent cells by boosting IL1A translation.
Laberge RM.sub: Buck Institute for Research on Aging (PubMed affiliation, 2015)
story: Remi-Martin Laberge was first author of a 2015 Nature Cell Biology paper in the Atlas (LAB2015), written at the Buck Institute with 20 co-authors. Old, non-dividing (senescent) cells release inflammatory signals called the SASP. The study found that mTOR switches on the production of IL1A, a cytokine near the top of that cascade, and that rapamycin shuts this down. In mice, rapamycin also stopped senescent cells from helping prostate tumours grow.

highlights.LAB2015: First author of the cell and mouse study linking mTOR, IL1A translation and the senescence secretory profile.

Lane CM.lab_name: Department of Cardiovascular Diseases, Mayo Clinic (Rochester, Minnesota, USA)
Lane CM.role: First author of a 2026 trial of low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
Lane CM.sub: Department of Cardiovascular Diseases, Mayo Clinic (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Conor M Lane was first author of a 2026 Mayo Clinic Proceedings paper in the Atlas (LAN2026). It tested low-dose rapamycin in frail older adults who have heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. The team included groups at Mayo Clinic and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The abstract was not yet available when the Atlas entry was made, so results are not summarised here.

highlights.LAN2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Cardiovascular Diseases at Mayo Clinic.

Landoas A.lab_name: Pharmacy Department, Grenoble Alpes University Hospital (Grenoble, France)
Landoas A.role: First author of a 2026 retrospective study of everolimus timing and chronic lung allograft dysfunction in lung transplant patients.
Landoas A.sub: Pharmacy Department, Grenoble Alpes University Hospital (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Agathe Landoas was first author of a 2026 study from Grenoble Alpes University Hospital (LANDOAS2026). It looked back at lung transplant patients who received everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor. Starting everolimus later, and stopping and restarting it more often, went with a higher risk of chronic lung allograft dysfunction. This was a single-centre review of records, so it cannot show cause and effect.

highlights.LANDOAS2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Pharmacy Department of Grenoble Alpes University Hospital.

Morita M.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry, McGill University (Montreal, Quebec, Canada)
Morita M.role: First author of a 2013 study showing that mTORC1 controls mitochondrial activity through 4E-BP-dependent translation.
Morita M.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Goodman Cancer Research Centre, McGill University (PubMed affiliation, 2013)
story: Masahiro Morita was first author of a 2013 Cell Metabolism paper from McGill University (MOR2013). The study found that mTORC1 helps cells build and run mitochondria by turning up the translation of mitochondria-related messenger RNAs, through the 4E-BP proteins. PubMed also lists a Masahiro Morita as second author of a 2012 metformin paper in the Atlas (LAR2012), but that record has no affiliation, so it is not counted here.

highlights.MOR2013: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Biochemistry and the Goodman Cancer Research Centre at McGill University.

Hakkola J.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
Hakkola J.role: Senior (last) author of a 2026 study of PXR-driven liver growth in healthy volunteers and mice, with AKT-MTOR activation in male mice.
Hakkola J.sub: Pharmacology and Toxicology, Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, University of Oulu (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Jukka Hakkola was last author of a 2026 study from the University of Oulu (LASSILA2026). In 16 healthy volunteers, one week of rifampicin raised the liver-to-body-weight ratio by 2.7 percent. In male mice, activating the same receptor (PXR) enlarged the liver and raised AKT-MTOR activity, without the YAP activation seen in earlier work. PubMed places the group at the Oulu research unit.

highlights.LASSILA2026: Last author; PubMed lists the author in the Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine at the University of Oulu.

Lassila P.lab_name: Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, Pharmacology and Toxicology, University of Oulu (Oulu, Finland)
Lassila P.role: First author of a 2026 study of PXR-driven liver growth in healthy volunteers and mice, with AKT-MTOR activation in male mice.
Lassila P.sub: Pharmacology and Toxicology, Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine, University of Oulu (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Piia Lassila was first author of a 2026 study from the University of Oulu (LASSILA2026). In 16 healthy volunteers, one week of rifampicin raised the liver-to-body-weight ratio by 2.7 percent. In male mice, activating the receptor PXR enlarged the liver and raised AKT-MTOR activity, but not YAP activity.

highlights.LASSILA2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Research Unit of Biomedicine and Internal Medicine at the University of Oulu.

Kim DJ.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Kim DJ.role: Co-author of three structural and cell-biology studies of the Rag GTPase-Ragulator system that recruits mTORC1 to the lysosome.
Kim DJ.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (PubMed affiliation, 2017–2019)
story: Do Jin Kim appears as a middle author on three Atlas papers from Berkeley, all about how mTORC1 is brought to the lysosome. In 2017 the group solved the structure of the Ragulator complex bound to the Rag proteins (SUX2017). In 2018 they showed that nutrients loosen the Rag-Ragulator grip so the Rags cycle on and off (LAW2018). In 2019 they published the structure of the folliculin complex, which acts as a checkpoint on Rag activation (LAW2019).
PubMed lists the author in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley, on all three papers.

highlights.SUX2017: Middle author of the Ragulator-RagA/C structure paper.
highlights.LAW2018: Middle author of the study of the nutrient-controlled Rag-Ragulator affinity switch.
highlights.LAW2019: Middle author of the folliculin-Rag cryo-EM structure paper.

Lim CY.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Lim CY.role: Co-author of two Berkeley studies, on the folliculin-Rag checkpoint (2019) and the LYCHOS cholesterol sensor (2022).
Lim CY.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (PubMed affiliation, 2019–2022)
story: Chun-Yan Lim is a middle author on two Atlas papers from the Berkeley group. The 2019 paper gave the structure of the lysosomal folliculin complex, a checkpoint that holds back Rag activation of mTORC1 (LAW2019). The 2022 paper found LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein that senses cholesterol and passes the signal to mTORC1 by sequestering the GATOR1 complex (SHI2022).
PubMed lists the author in the Department of Molecular and Cell Biology at the University of California, Berkeley, on both.

highlights.LAW2019: Middle author of the folliculin-Rag cryo-EM structure paper.
highlights.SHI2022: Middle author of the study that identified LYCHOS as a cholesterol sensor for mTORC1.

Lee JH.lab_name: Laboratory of Gene Regulation and Signal Transduction, Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, University of California San Diego (La Jolla, California, USA)
Lee JH.role: First author of a 2010 fruit fly study of Sestrin as a feedback inhibitor of TOR that guards against age-related damage.
Lee JH.sub: Department of Pharmacology, University of California San Diego School of Medicine (PubMed affiliation, 2010)
story: Jun Hee Lee was first author of a 2010 Science paper in the Atlas (LEE2010), listed at the University of California San Diego. In fruit flies, Sestrin rises when TOR stays active, and then pushes TOR back down. Flies without Sestrin built up fat and developed mitochondrial, muscle and heart problems that looked like ageing. Blocking TOR or switching on AMPK prevented these problems.

highlights.LEE2010: First author of the fruit fly study on Sestrin and TOR feedback.

Lee DJW.lab_name: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (Singapore)
Lee DJW.role: First author of a 2024 systematic review of rapamycin and its derivatives for ageing-related changes in humans.
Lee DJW.sub: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, National University of Singapore (PubMed affiliation, 2024)
story: Deborah J W Lee was first author of a 2024 Lancet Healthy Longevity systematic review in the Atlas (LEE2024), with two co-authors. The team searched five databases and found 18,400 papers, of which 19 studies were included. Rapamycin and related drugs improved some immune, heart and skin measures, with no clear effect on hormones, muscle or the nervous system. Infections and blood fats rose in people who already had age-related disease.

highlights.LEE2024: First author of the systematic review; PubMed lists the author at the National University of Singapore.

Lee SY.lab_name: Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science (Daejeon, South Korea)
Lee SY.role: First author of a 2026 mouse study showing that ectopic ERBB4 in excitatory neurons drives Alzheimer's-like changes through mTOR signalling.
Lee SY.sub: Center for Vascular Research, Institute for Basic Science, and KAIST (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Se Young Lee was first author of a 2026 Nature paper in the Atlas (LEE2026), with 12 co-authors from IBS, KAIST and UNIST in Korea. In Alzheimer's disease mice, excitatory neurons switched on the gene Erbb4 early. Removing it protected against synapse loss, plaques and memory problems, and adding it to normal mice reproduced most of the damage, though not the plaques. These effects needed mTOR signalling downstream of ERBB4.

highlights.LEE2026: First author; PubMed lists the author at the Center for Vascular Research of the Institute for Basic Science and in the Department of Biological Sciences at KAIST.

Lei HT.lab_name: Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute (Ashburn, Virginia, USA)
Lei HT.role: First author of a 2018 crystal structure of arginine-bound SLC38A9, the lysosomal arginine transporter linked to mTORC1.
Lei HT.sub: Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute (PubMed affiliation, 2018)
story: Hsiang-Ting Lei was first author of a 2018 paper in Nature Structural and Molecular Biology (LEI2018), with three co-authors. The team solved the crystal structure of zebrafish SLC38A9 holding an arginine molecule. SLC38A9 sits on the lysosome and helps tell mTORC1 which amino acids are available, so the structure shows how that binding works.

highlights.LEI2018: First author of the SLC38A9 arginine crystal structure; PubMed lists the work at the Janelia Research Campus.

Lelegren M.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Lelegren M.role: First author of a 2016 study of how rapamycin changes protein-quality-control systems in marmoset liver, muscle and fat.
Lelegren M.sub: Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (PubMed affiliation, 2016)
story: Matthew Lelegren was first author of a 2016 paper on marmosets treated with rapamycin (LEL2016), from the Barshop Institute in San Antonio. In liver and muscle, rapamycin went with more of a core proteasome subunit, although proteasome activity did not change. Helper proteins in mitochondria rose in muscle but not liver, and autophagy rose in muscle and fat but not liver. The effects depended on the tissue.

highlights.LEL2016: First author; PubMed lists the author at the South Texas Veterans Health Care System and the Barshop Institute.

Ross C.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Ross C.role: Author of three marmoset rapamycin studies: first author of the 2015 metabolic study and co-author of the 2014 and 2016 papers.
Ross C.sub: Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio; Texas A&M University San Antonio (PubMed affiliation, 2014–2016)
story: Corinna Ross was first author of the 2015 Atlas study of long-term rapamycin in common marmosets (ROS2015). Body weight, activity, blood fats and glucose handling barely changed, so the metabolic side effects were small. Ross is also a co-author of the 2014 paper that first described dosing and blood levels of rapamycin in marmosets (TAR2014), and of the 2016 paper on proteasome and autophagy changes in the same animals (LEL2016).
PubMed lists the author at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio on all three, and at Texas A&M University San Antonio on the first two.

highlights.ROS2015: First author of the study of metabolic effects of long-term rapamycin in marmosets.
highlights.TAR2014: Second author of the paper that first described rapamycin dosing in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Middle author of the marmoset proteostasis study.

Tardif S.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Tardif S.role: First author of the 2014 marmoset rapamycin dosing study and senior author of the 2015 marmoset metabolic study, plus co-author of a 2016 follow-up.
Tardif S.sub: Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio; Southwest National Primate Research Center (PubMed affiliation, 2014–2016)
story: Suzette Tardif was first author of the 2014 Atlas paper that first described how to dose rapamycin in the common marmoset (TAR2014). Oral rapamycin reached blood levels like those used in mouse and human work, and it lowered mTORC1 signalling in tissues. Tardif was last author of the 2015 follow-up, which found only minor metabolic effects of long-term treatment (ROS2015), and is a co-author of the 2016 study on proteasome and autophagy changes (LEL2016).
PubMed lists the author at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio and at the Southwest National Primate Research Center on these papers.

highlights.TAR2014: First author of the marmoset rapamycin dosing and tolerability study.
highlights.ROS2015: Last author of the study of metabolic effects of long-term rapamycin in marmosets.
highlights.LEL2016: Co-author of the marmoset proteostasis study.

Wang Zhenhai.lab_name: Neurology Center, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (Yinchuan, Ningxia, China)
Wang Zhenhai.role: Senior (last) author of a 2026 cell study on Brucella suis strain 2, macrophage polarisation, autophagy and PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling.
Wang Zhenhai.sub: Neurology Center, General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Zhenhai Wang was last author of a 2026 study in the Journal of Medical Microbiology (LI2026B), written with four co-authors in Ningxia, China. In cultured BV2 microglia-like cells, the vaccine strain Brucella suis S2 pushed cells into a mixed M1/M2 state and switched on autophagy. The M2 state and autophagy together helped the bacteria multiply inside cells, through PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling. This was cell work, not an animal or human study.

highlights.LI2026B: Last author; PubMed lists the author at the Neurology Center and the Institute of Medical Sciences of the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University.

Liang X.lab_name: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (Taiyuan, Shanxi, China)
Liang X.role: First author of a 2026 study of how the lncRNA LINP1 binds mTOR and limits radiation-induced senescence in skin cells.
Liang X.sub: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Xiaoting Liang was first author of a 2026 study in Molecular and Cellular Biochemistry (LIANG2026). The long non-coding RNA LINP1 rises after radiation and binds the FAT domain of mTOR. That weakens the contact between mTOR and p53, so less p53 is phosphorylated and fewer skin cells turn senescent. The team tested keratinocytes and human skin samples kept in the lab.

highlights.LIANG2026: First author; PubMed lists the author at Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan.

Li N.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine (New Haven, Connecticut, USA)
Li N.role: First author of a 2010 rat study showing that ketamine's fast antidepressant effects need mTOR-dependent synapse formation.
Li N.sub: Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine (PubMed affiliation, 2010)
story: Nanxin Li was first author of a 2010 Science paper in the Atlas (LIX2010), from the Yale psychiatry group. In rats, ketamine quickly switched on mTOR in the prefrontal cortex and led to new synaptic spines. Blocking mTOR with rapamycin stopped both the new synapses and the antidepressant-like behaviour. This was animal work, and it points to a mechanism rather than proving the same steps in depressed patients.

highlights.LIX2010: First author of the rat study linking ketamine, mTOR and synapse formation.

Wullschleger S.role: First author of a 2006 review in Cell on TOR signalling in growth and metabolism.
story: Stephan Wullschleger was first author of the 2006 review "TOR signaling in growth and metabolism" in Cell (WUL2006), written with two co-authors at the Biozentrum in Basel. It lays out the two mammalian TOR complexes, TORC1 (rapamycin sensitive) and TORC2 (not), and what each controls. A Stephan Wullschleger is also a middle author of the 2002 TOR complexes paper in the Atlas (LOE2002), but that record has no affiliation, so it is not counted here.

highlights.WUL2006: First author of the review; PubMed lists the author at the Biozentrum, University of Basel.

Löffler AS.lab_name: Department of Internal Medicine I, University of Tübingen (Tübingen, Germany)
Löffler AS.role: First author of a 2011 study showing that ULK1 phosphorylates AMPK and so forms a negative feedback loop.
Löffler AS.sub: Department of Internal Medicine I, University of Tübingen (PubMed affiliation, 2011)
story: Antje S Löffler was first author of a 2011 paper in Autophagy (LOF2011), from the University of Tübingen. AMPK was known to switch on ULK1 to start autophagy. The study found that ULK1 and ULK2 also phosphorylate all three AMPK subunits and reduce its activity, so the two kinases regulate each other in a feedback loop. The work used cultured cells.

highlights.LOF2011: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Internal Medicine I at the University of Tübingen.

Lv S.lab_name: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Lv S.role: First author of a 2026 study of how USP7 stabilises KDM5B, lowers TSC1 and activates mTOR to drive kidney fibrosis.
Lv S.sub: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Shiqi Lv was first author of a 2026 paper in Molecular Biomedicine (LV2026S) from Zhongshan Hospital in Shanghai. USP7 was raised in kidneys from people with chronic kidney disease. In two mouse models of kidney injury, USP7 kept the enzyme KDM5B from being degraded, which turned down TSC1 and let mTOR switch on and scar tissue form. Blocking USP7 genetically or with a drug reversed this in mice.

highlights.LV2026S: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Nephrology at Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University.

Zhang Xiaoyan.lab_name: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Zhang Xiaoyan.role: Senior (last) author of a 2026 study of how USP7 stabilises KDM5B, lowers TSC1 and activates mTOR to drive kidney fibrosis.
Zhang Xiaoyan.sub: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Xiaoyan Zhang was last author of a 2026 paper in Molecular Biomedicine (LV2026S) from Zhongshan Hospital in Shanghai, with 13 authors in all. The study found USP7 raised in kidneys from people with chronic kidney disease. In mice, USP7 stabilised KDM5B, which lowered TSC1, activated mTOR and promoted fibrosis. Blocking USP7 reduced fibrosis in both mouse injury models.

highlights.LV2026S: Last author; PubMed lists the group in the Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University.

Feng H.lab_name: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou, Jiangsu, China)
Feng H.role: Senior (last) author of a 2026 study of PIP4K2A, AKT/mTOR signalling and autophagy after cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
Feng H.sub: Department of Neurology, Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Hongxuan Feng was last author of a 2026 paper in Translational Stroke Research (MA2026), with 11 authors from the neurology department in Suzhou. In mice and cultured neurons, raising PIP4K2A reduced stroke-like brain injury. It lowered the TRIB3-p62 complex, improved autophagic flux and went with stronger AKT/mTOR signalling. The authors note that the small patient group in the study cannot show cause or tissue of origin.

highlights.MA2026: Last author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Neurology of the Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University.

Ma B.lab_name: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou, Jiangsu, China)
Ma B.role: First author of a 2026 study of PIP4K2A, AKT/mTOR signalling and autophagy after cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
Ma B.sub: Department of Neurology, Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Bodun Ma was first author of a 2026 paper in Translational Stroke Research (MA2026). In mice and cultured neurons, raising PIP4K2A reduced injury after a temporary loss of blood flow to the brain. It lowered the TRIB3-p62 complex, improved autophagic flux and went with stronger AKT/mTOR signalling. The patient data in the paper came from a small group, so they are only a hint.

highlights.MA2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Neurology of the Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University.

Elshal M.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (Mansoura, Egypt)
Elshal M.role: Senior (last) author of a 2026 rat study of carvedilol, seizure development and PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related changes.
Elshal M.sub: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Mahmoud Elshal was last author of a 2026 paper in Scientific Reports (MADKOUR2026), a four-author study from Mansoura University. In rats given repeated PTZ to model epilepsy development, carvedilol went with lower seizure scores, less hippocampal damage and less NLRP3-linked inflammation, along with changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related proteins. The authors state that this does not prove the pathway is the cause.

highlights.MADKOUR2026: Last author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology at Mansoura University.

Madkour AH.lab_name: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (Mansoura, Egypt)
Madkour AH.role: First author of a 2026 rat study of carvedilol, seizure development and PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related changes.
Madkour AH.sub: Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, Mansoura University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Ahmed H Madkour was first author of a 2026 paper in Scientific Reports (MADKOUR2026) from Mansoura University. In rats given repeated PTZ to model epilepsy development, carvedilol went with lower seizure scores, less hippocampal damage and less inflammation, along with changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related proteins. The authors say the study shows associations, not a proven pathway-specific cause.

highlights.MADKOUR2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology at Mansoura University.

Majumder PK.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Majumder PK.role: First author of a 2004 mouse study showing that mTOR inhibition reverses AKT-driven prostate neoplasia.
Majumder PK.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Harvard Medical School (PubMed affiliation, 2004)
story: Pradip K Majumder was first author of a 2004 Nature Medicine paper in the Atlas (MAJ2004), with 12 co-authors. Mice made to express active human AKT1 in the prostate developed early prostate cancer-like growth. Treating them with an mTOR inhibitor (RAD001) killed the abnormal cells and reversed the growth. The paper also found that HIF-1 alpha targets and BCL2 could help tumours resist such treatment.

highlights.MAJ2004: First author; PubMed lists the author at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School.

Manifava M.lab_name: Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute (Cambridge, United Kingdom)
Manifava M.role: First author of a 2016 live-imaging study of how fast mTORC1 moves to lysosomes after amino acids are added.
story: Maria Manifava was first author of a 2016 eLife paper in the Atlas (MAN2016), from the Babraham Institute in Cambridge. Live imaging of human cells showed mTORC1 reaching lysosomes within about 2 minutes of adding amino acids, peaking by 5 minutes. The signal to its usual targets came later, which suggests mTORC1 visits the lysosome briefly and then acts elsewhere.

highlights.MAN2016: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Signalling Programme at the Babraham Institute.

Quinn D.role: Co-author of two clinical trials of mTOR inhibitors for immune function in older adults (2018 and 2021).
Quinn D.sub: resTORbio (Boston) and P3 Research, Wellington, New Zealand (PubMed affiliation, 2018–2021)
story: Dean Quinn is a middle author on two Atlas trial papers about low-dose mTOR inhibitors in older adults. The 2018 phase 2a trial of 264 people found fewer reported infections over the next year with a BEZ235 plus everolimus combination (MAN2018). The 2021 phase 2b and phase 3 trials of RTB101 gave mixed results: a lower infection rate in one pooled analysis, but no benefit in the phase 3 trial (MAN2021).
PubMed lists the author at P3 Research in Wellington, New Zealand, on both papers, and at resTORbio on the 2021 one.

highlights.MAN2018: Middle author of the phase 2a trial; PubMed lists the author at P3 Research in Wellington.
highlights.MAN2021: Middle author of the phase 2b and phase 3 trials; PubMed lists the author at resTORbio and P3 Research.

Shergill S.role: Senior (last) author of the 2021 phase 2b and phase 3 trials of the mTOR inhibitor RTB101 in older adults.
story: Sarb Shergill was last author of a 2021 Lancet Healthy Longevity paper in the Atlas (MAN2021), with seven co-authors listed at resTORbio. It reports two trials of RTB101, a drug that blocks mTOR, given daily for 16 weeks to adults over 65. In the phase 2b trial, fewer people on 10 mg had a lab-confirmed respiratory infection, but the result came from a pooled analysis and the corrected analysis was not significant. The phase 3 trial showed no drop in respiratory illness.

highlights.MAN2021: Last author; PubMed lists the author at resTORbio in Boston.

Marchant ED.lab_name: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Long School of Medicine, University of Texas at San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Marchant ED.role: First author of a 2026 mouse study of constitutive mTORC1 activation in skeletal muscle, inflammation and glucose tolerance.
Marchant ED.sub: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, University of Texas at San Antonio (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Erik D Marchant was first author of a 2026 paper in Function (MARCHANT2026), from the Barshop Institute and Long School of Medicine in San Antonio. Mice lacking the GATOR1 component Depdc5 in muscle had constantly active mTORC1. Their muscle showed more inflammation, but glucose tolerance stayed normal, even on a Western diet. The result questions the idea that muscle mTORC1 overactivity alone causes insulin resistance.

highlights.MARCHANT2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology and the Barshop Institute at the University of Texas at San Antonio.

Anderson RM.lab_name: Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
Anderson RM.role: Senior (last) author of a 2017 comparison of the NIA and Wisconsin calorie restriction studies in rhesus monkeys.
Anderson RM.sub: Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin; William S. Middleton Memorial Veterans Hospital (PubMed affiliation, 2017)
story: Rozalyn M Anderson was last author of a 2017 Nature Communications paper in the Atlas (MAT2017), with nine co-authors. It compared the long-running calorie restriction studies in rhesus monkeys run by the National Institute on Aging and by the University of Wisconsin. Taken together, they support health benefits of calorie restriction in monkeys. Whether survival improved depended on study design, such as when restriction began and what the control diet contained.

highlights.MAT2017: Last author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Medicine at the University of Wisconsin and at the Middleton Veterans Hospital.

de Cabo R.lab_name: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
de Cabo R.role: Co-author of the 2017 comparison of the NIA and Wisconsin calorie restriction studies in rhesus monkeys.
de Cabo R.sub: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging (PubMed affiliation, 2017)
story: Rafael de Cabo is a middle author of the 2017 Nature Communications paper in the Atlas that compared two long calorie restriction studies in rhesus monkeys (MAT2017). The paper found consistent health benefits, while the effect on survival depended on study design and control diet. PubMed lists the author at the Translational Gerontology Branch of the National Institute on Aging on this paper.
De Cabo also appears in two mouse lifespan papers in the Atlas (STR2012, MIL2011), but those PubMed records give no affiliation for this author, so they are not counted here.

highlights.MAT2017: Middle author; PubMed lists the author at the Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging.

Ma XM.lab_name: Department of Research Oncology Diagnostics, Genentech (South San Francisco, California, USA)
Ma XM.role: First author of a 2009 review on mTOR-mediated control of translation.
Ma XM.sub: Department of Research Oncology Diagnostics, Genentech (PubMed affiliation, 2009)
story: Xiaoju Max Ma was first author of the 2009 Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology review "Molecular mechanisms of mTOR-mediated translational control" (MAX2009), written with John Blenis. It explains how mTOR senses nutrients, energy, stress and growth signals and passes them on to control protein synthesis. A Xiaoju Max Ma is also a middle author of the 2011 Grb10 paper in the Atlas (YUX2011), but that record has no affiliation, so it is not counted here.

highlights.MAX2009: First author of the review; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Research Oncology Diagnostics at Genentech.

McNeill M.lab_name: Division of Hematology-Oncology, Department of Pediatrics, The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto, Ontario, Canada)
McNeill M.role: First author of a 2026 retrospective study of sirolimus in children with Evans syndrome and related autoimmune cytopenias.
McNeill M.sub: Division of Hematology-Oncology, The Hospital for Sick Children, and University of Toronto (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Maggie McNeill was first author of a 2026 paper in the British Journal of Haematology (MCNEILL2026), from The Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto. The team looked back at children with Evans syndrome and related autoimmune blood-cell problems who took sirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor. They report that it was effective. The abstract was not yet indexed when the Atlas entry was made, so numbers are not given here.

highlights.MCNEILL2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Division of Hematology-Oncology at The Hospital for Sick Children and the University of Toronto.

Meikle L.lab_name: Division of Translational Medicine, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Meikle L.role: First author of a 2008 mouse study showing that rapamycin and RAD001 rescue a neuronal model of tuberous sclerosis.
Meikle L.sub: Division of Translational Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School (PubMed affiliation, 2008)
story: Lynsey Meikle was first author of a 2008 Journal of Neuroscience paper in the Atlas (MEI2008), with six co-authors. Mice lacking Tsc1 in neurons are a model of tuberous sclerosis in the brain. Treating them with rapamycin or RAD001 raised median survival from 33 days to over 100 days and improved behaviour and cell size, though some abnormal neuron features remained. The work was in mice.

highlights.MEI2008: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Division of Translational Medicine at Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School.

Melendez A.lab_name: Department of Medicine, Columbia University College of Physicians & Surgeons (New York, New York, USA)
Melendez A.role: First author of a 2003 C. elegans study showing that autophagy genes are needed for dauer formation and lifespan extension.
Melendez A.sub: Department of Medicine, Columbia University College of Physicians & Surgeons (PubMed affiliation, 2003)
story: Alicia Meléndez was first author of a 2003 Science paper in the Atlas (MEL2003), with five co-authors. In the roundworm C. elegans, animals with reduced insulin-like signalling normally live longer. Worms lacking the autophagy gene bec-1 lost that extra lifespan and could not form dauer larvae properly. The study showed that autophagy is required for these effects in worms.

highlights.MEL2003: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University.

Goodarzi H.lab_name: Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, University of California, San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Goodarzi H.role: Co-author of two studies, on a bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor in breast cancer (2023) and on SLC15A3 and mTORC1 in lymphoma (2026).
Goodarzi H.sub: Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, UCSF; Arc Institute (PubMed affiliation, 2023–2026)
story: Hani Goodarzi is a middle author on two Atlas papers with UCSF groups. The 2023 paper tested RMC-6272, a drug that blocks mTORC1 much more than mTORC2, and found it killed ER-positive breast cancer cells and overcame resistance to other therapies in cells and patient-derived tumours in mice (MEN2023). The 2026 paper showed that the dipeptide transporter SLC15A3 keeps mTORC1 active in lymphoma cells that resist antimetabolite chemotherapy, and that those resistant cells were sensitive to rapamycin (YAN2026).
PubMed lists the author in the Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics at UCSF on both, and at the Arc Institute on the 2026 paper.

highlights.MEN2023: Middle author of the bi-steric mTORC1 inhibitor study in breast cancer.
highlights.YAN2026: Middle author of the SLC15A3 lymphoma study; PubMed also lists the author at the Arc Institute.

Meng D.lab_name: Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, University of California San Francisco (San Francisco, California, USA)
Meng D.role: First author of a 2023 study of RMC-6272, a bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor, in drug-resistant breast cancer.
Meng D.sub: Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, UCSF (PubMed affiliation, 2023)
story: Delong Meng was first author of a 2023 Oncogene paper in the Atlas (MEN2023), from UCSF with colleagues at Revolution Medicines. RMC-6272 blocks mTORC1 more than 25 times more strongly than mTORC2. It killed ER-positive breast cancer cell lines, especially those with PIK3CA or PTEN mutations, and still worked in hormone-therapy-resistant and CDK4/6-inhibitor-resistant models. The work used cell lines and tumours grown from patients in mice.

highlights.MEN2023: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences at UCSF.

Yang YC.role: Co-author of two papers on the bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitors RMC-6272 (2023) and RMC-5552 (2025).
story: Yu Chi Yang is a middle author on two Atlas papers about bi-steric drugs that block mTORC1 more than mTORC2. The 2023 preclinical paper showed RMC-6272 overcame resistance in breast cancer cells and mouse tumours (MEN2023). The 2025 phase 1 trial of RMC-5552 in 57 people with advanced solid tumours had low rates of high blood sugar and a 64 percent disease control rate (SCH2025). That trial had no comparison group.
PubMed lists the author in the Department of Biology at Revolution Medicines on the first paper and at Revolution Medicines on the second.

highlights.MEN2023: Middle author; PubMed lists the affiliation as the Department of Biology at Revolution Medicines.
highlights.SCH2025: Middle author of the phase 1 trial; PubMed lists Revolution Medicines.
